claim: Vaccination fails to prevent smallpox and is itself dangerous, so compulsory laws should be repealed.
what_happened: Mass vaccination drove smallpox to global eradication in 1980; unvaccinated antis kept dying of it in the meantime.
lesson: Organised resistance can riot and still lose to a product whose results are visible in the body count; publish the outcomes, not the arguments.

quotes.text: FALSE CLAIMS FOR VACCINATION EXPOSED ITS FAILURES AND DANGERS ESTABLISHED
quotes.speaker: Mr. Higgins (letter)

quotes.text: ANTI-VACCINATIONIST DIES. Submits to Inoculation Only After Smallpox Hud Attacked Him.
He wants : the anti-vaccinatiphists to prove : the truth of their theories or keep : still.
quotes.speaker: Health Commissioner Hall

claim: Being vaccinated drives people insane or to suicide.
what_happened: Single anecdotes of illness after a shot were coincidence; no link between smallpox vaccine and insanity was ever established.
lesson: When millions adopt something, some will fall ill afterwards by chance; expect anecdote headlines and answer them with base rates.

quotes.text: VACCINATION CAUSES INSANITY. Martha Hitter Said to Have Lost Her Mind Through Inoculation.
BLAMED VACCINATION

claim: Doctors only push vaccination because they profit from performing it.
what_happened: Doctors earned far more treating smallpox than preventing it; the Lancet pointed out the vaccination fee was a pittance by comparison.
lesson: 'They only sell it to make money' is answered by showing the seller would earn more if the product failed.

quotes.text: One of the favorite statements of the anti-vaccinationists is that medical men support vaccination because they profit by performing the operation.

claim: The Salk vaccine was rushed into use in violation of normal medical procedure.
what_happened: The Cutter Laboratories batch caused about 40,000 polio cases weeks before this charge, a real failure; the vaccine itself worked and US polio collapsed within a decade.
lesson: Speed critics are sometimes pointing at a real manufacturing failure; fix the quality control loudly rather than denying the rush.

quotes.text: Confusion Over Vaccine Blamed On Undue Hurry
was rushed Into use in violation of normal medical procedures
quotes.speaker: Dr. Julian Price, AMA

claim: Vaccinating children against rubella may be misdirected; better to let them catch it for natural immunity.
what_happened: Routine childhood rubella vaccination eliminated endemic rubella and congenital rubella syndrome in the US by 2004.
lesson: Expert doubt about a new rollout is a reason to measure, not to stop; let the data settle it.

quotes.text: Value of Measles Vaccine Is Doubted

claim: Moderna's ambitious mRNA platform keeps hitting hurdles and losing executives.
what_happened: Two years later Moderna's mRNA COVID vaccine was authorised and given to hundreds of millions of people.
lesson: A platform's track record of setbacks says little about what happens when the right problem arrives for it.

quotes.text: But Moderna’s ambitious goals have run into hurdles in the past.

claim: A pure flying machine is impossible; the machines being built do not fly.
what_happened: The Wrights flew at Kitty Hawk on 17 December 1903, about two months after the New York Times editorial.
lesson: 'It can't be done' from people not doing it is the cheapest kind of verdict; watch the builders, not the editorials.

quotes.text: 1888: A Pure Flying Machine is Impossible
1903: Flying Machines Which Do Not Fly

claim: The aeroplane is doomed because women will never accept the hideous costumes flying requires.
what_happened: Flying needed no special costume once cabins were enclosed; women became a large share of air travellers.
lesson: A current form-factor problem is not a market verdict; the awkward part is usually the first thing engineering removes.

quotes.text: The possibile popularity of the aeroplane is doomed. It can never have the support of the feminine sei
1909: No Chance for the Aeroplane

claim: The aeroplane will be nothing but a fad; the future of aerial navigation is the dirigible.
what_happened: Dirigibles peaked in the 1930s and died with the Hindenburg in 1937; fixed-wing aircraft took over all air travel.
lesson: Experts often bet on the more mature-looking rival technology; the one with the steeper improvement curve usually wins.

quotes.text: CALLS AEROPLANES A fAD Cornell Professor Pins His Faith to Dlrlfllbies.
quotes.speaker: Prof. J. C. McDermott, Cornell

quotes.text: AEROPLANES ONLY A FAD

claim: Flying across the Atlantic is impossible and foolhardy with any aeroplane that can be built.
what_happened: Alcock and Brown flew nonstop across the Atlantic in June 1919, five years after Orville Wright's dismissal.
lesson: Even the inventor judges by today's engine; a hard limit stated in terms of current hardware tends to fall within a decade.

quotes.text: WRIGHT CALLS OCEAN FLIGHT IMPOSSIBLE
quotes.speaker: Orville Wright

quotes.text: 1 cannot do so and neither can any other aeroplane manufacturer who will, speak frankly.
quotes.speaker: Orville Wright

claim: Aviators are dying almost weekly; the sacrifice of human life to flying is not worth it.
what_happened: Early flying really was lethal for its pilots; regulation, engineering and enclosed airliners made commercial flying the safest way to travel.
lesson: Early casualties are real and should drive safety engineering, but they say little about what the mature version's risk will be.

quotes.text: Scarcely ft week passes but the newspapers arc called on to record the death o ono or more navigators of the air.
"COME DOWN!" CRY SPECTATORS

claim: Flying and motoring produce new diseases and disfigurements such as the 'aeroplane face'.
what_happened: No 'aeroplane face' or motor disease entered medicine; the named conditions vanished with open cockpits and goggles.
lesson: A novel bodily sensation gets a disease name early; most such names do not survive the first generation of users.

quotes.text: 1908: Now the 'Aeroplane Face'
1910: A NEW AUTOMOBILE AND AEROPLANE DISEASE

claim: Machine-made ice is inferior to natural ice; nature's ice is germ-free and cannot be beaten.
what_happened: Natural ice, often cut from polluted rivers, was the real typhoid risk; plant ice and then the home refrigerator wiped out the natural ice trade by the 1930s.
lesson: When the incumbent's pitch shifts to 'natural is purer', it has usually lost on cost and is fighting on feeling.

quotes.text: NATURAL ICE IS FREE OF GERMS
You can not beat nature; nor can you approach if for it is perfection.
Artificial Ice Not Inferior.

claim: Sliced bread is a lazy fad that will wear itself out like miniature golf.
what_happened: Sliced bread became the default loaf in America within a decade and the byword for a good invention.
lesson: Convenience mocked as laziness is usually just convenience; bet on the thing that saves a daily chore.

quotes.text: These 'lazy sliced bread devotees are. tantalizingly vague about It till, too.
quotes.speaker: letter writer

quotes.text: Slice Bread is lazy

claim: Coffee drinking causes heart attacks and heart disease.
what_happened: Later large cohorts that controlled for smoking found moderate coffee neutral or protective for the heart.
lesson: A single observational study is a lead, not a verdict; confounders like smoking reverse many early health scares.

quotes.text: New Study Links Coffee Drinking To Heart Affacks
Study links coffee to heart disease

claim: Coffee drinking may account for a large share of pancreatic cancer.
what_happened: The Harvard team's own follow-up failed to replicate it, and later studies found no link.
lesson: A prestigious name on a scary study raises its reach, not its truth; wait for replication.

quotes.text: Harvard Study Links Coffee Consumption To Pancreatic Cancer

claim: Coffee raises blood cholesterol.
what_happened: Unfiltered coffee does raise LDL through cafestol; paper-filtered coffee largely does not.
lesson: Many scares hide a real mechanism under the wrong headline; find the narrow true part and design around it.

quotes.text: Study links coffee high blood cholesterol

claim: Drinking five or more cups of coffee a day raises lung cancer risk.
what_happened: The association was explained by heavy coffee drinkers also being smokers.
lesson: When a habit travels with another, check which one the harm belongs to before acting on it.

quotes.text: Study links Coffee and lung cancer

claim: Coffee blocks iron, thins women's bones and may cause rheumatoid arthritis.
what_happened: Coffee does reduce iron absorption with meals and slightly affects calcium; the arthritis and broad osteoporosis scares did not hold up as major risks.
lesson: A product used by everyone accumulates a long list of weak harms; rank them by size before reacting.

quotes.text: Study links coffee to iron deficiency in women
Study Links Coffee Osteoporosis
Study links coffee to form of arthritis

claim: Excessive salt intake may be causing the epidemic of high blood pressure.
what_happened: Salt reduction became WHO policy; high sodium intake is an established cause of hypertension and cardiovascular deaths.
lesson: A health warning backed by a controlled trial and a dose-response mechanism deserves more weight than one from a single cohort.

quotes.text: Salt linked to high blood pressure

claim: Football maims players and demoralises the young; legislatures should ban it.
what_happened: Deaths forced the 1906 rule changes rather than a ban; the game became huge, and repeated head injury (CTE) proved a real long-term harm.
lesson: A real harm with a popular product tends to end in rule changes, not bans; build the safety fix before regulators write it for you.

quotes.text: AGAINST FOOTBALL.
No game should be allowed to exist under those conditions.

claim: Competitive basketball harms the nervous feminine nature and tends to unsex girls.
what_happened: Girls' and women's basketball became one of the most played school sports with no such harm.
lesson: Fears framed around who 'should' use a thing tend to age worst; the excluded group usually becomes a core market.

quotes.text: AGAINST BASKETBALL.
quotes.speaker: Lucille E. Hill, Wellesley College

quotes.text: it lends to unsex the player
quotes.speaker: Lucille E. Hill, Wellesley College

claim: The new faster game without the centre jump strains boys' hearts to a dangerous degree.
what_happened: The centre-jump rule stayed gone and fast basketball became standard; no heart epidemic among players followed.
lesson: Sketchy early experiments get headlines; ask whether the measurement could separate effort from harm.

quotes.text: these sketchy experiments -! indicate the game is too fast iur ..,)st boys
quotes.speaker: Dr. Marcus Hobart, Northwestern

claim: For a few per cent of runners, jogging becomes a dangerous negative addiction.
what_happened: Exercise dependence is a recognised but rare condition; running's overall health benefit was confirmed many times over.
lesson: A small harmed minority is worth a feature that protects them, not a reason to doubt the product for the majority.

quotes.text: Jogging addiction dangerous: Expert
quotes.speaker: Prof. Michael Sachs

claim: Roller skating deforms children's limbs and gait.
what_happened: Roller skating went through repeated booms for a century with no limb deformities attributed to it.
lesson: Claims of physical deformity from a new pastime almost never survive; look for the injury data, not the anatomy theory.

quotes.text: ROLLER SKATING. Its Devotees A ro Uabte to Deformities ot the tlraibs and Other Fanottonil Derangements.

claim: Roller rinks are a new form of vice and endanger personal morals.
what_happened: Rinks became ordinary family venues; the moral panic passed within the decade.
lesson: A place where young people mix freely draws a morals panic first; it is a sign of demand, not of doom.

quotes.text: THE MORALE OF ROLLER-SKATING.
There seems to be an almost unanimous crusade against the roller-skate determined on by the pul

claim: Labor-saving inventions are making people lazy, soft and physically unfit.
what_happened: Physical inactivity did become a major public-health problem, but the moral collapse predicted did not, and freed time went to work, school and leisure.
lesson: Every convenience removes some effort people later miss; build the product and expect a market for putting the effort back.

quotes.text: It is a lazy, llator savinlg age.
Laziness Growing Sin, Learned Doctor Says
quotes.speaker: Dr. Joseph H. Barach

quotes.text: PERILS OF THE LAZY AGE.

claim: Every tool of civilisation costs a native skill: the coach the use of feet, the watch the skill of telling time by the sun.
what_happened: The skills did fade, as predicted, but almost nobody missed them; the tools freed attention for other things.
lesson: 'It will cost us a skill' is usually true and usually not a reason to stop; ask whether the lost skill still pays.

quotes.text: Tlie civilized man" has built a coach lAit I H has lost the use ofhis feet.

claim: Electricity doing the housework will make the housewife lazy and fat.
what_happened: Electrified homes freed hours of drudgery and helped women move into paid work, not idleness.
lesson: Time saved by a tool is rarely wasted at scale; it gets redeployed in ways the critics don't foresee.

quotes.text: No doubt if electricity continues to develop as it has during the past, decade, there will be no housekeepers in America,
quotes.speaker: James E. Davidson, NELA

thing: the can opener and telephone ordering
claim: Home baking is a lost art because the housewife now needs only a telephone and a can opener.
what_happened: Home baking did shrink sharply as commercial bread and canned food won; it survives as a hobby rather than a necessity.
lesson: A displaced chore often returns as a premium hobby; the convenience product and the craft product can both be businesses.

quotes.text: CAN OPENER AND TELEPHONE BLAMED , FOR LOST ART OF. BAKING IN HOMES
quotes.speaker: Magistrate Rudich

claim: With Velcro shoes, children won't learn to tie their laces or develop motor skills.
what_happened: Velcro became standard on toddler shoes, and children went on learning to tie laces when they moved to laced shoes.
lesson: A tool that delays a skill is not one that destroys it; people learn the skill when they need it.

quotes.text: 1984: With Velcro, kids not learning to ties shoes
But the often painstaking ritual of learning to tie one's shoes seems to have been booted into extinction replaced by the new Velcro fasteners.
quotes.speaker: Jewell Cardwell

claim: Pocket calculators make us dumb; students must be banned from them to learn arithmetic.
what_happened: Calculators became standard in schools and exams; mental arithmetic weakened somewhat, but maths education moved on to higher skills.
lesson: Schools ban a cognitive tool first and then teach with it; build for the second phase.

quotes.text: 1977: 'Modern Gadgets Make Us Dumb'
School bans calculators

claim: Pocket calculators can't beat the abacus or the slide rule, whose batteries never run out.
what_happened: The slide rule was extinct by the end of the 1970s and the abacus survives as a teaching tool.
lesson: A skilled user of the old tool can beat the new one in a demo; the market is decided by the unskilled user.

quotes.text: 1976: 'Pocket Calculators Can't Beat Ancient Chinese Abacus'
1984: 'Slide rule "fast as calculator" and batteries won't run out'

claim: The computer threatens the bookkeeper's trade and the comptometer operator.
what_happened: Comptometer operators vanished entirely; bookkeeping clerks shrank slowly but still numbered over a million decades later, doing different work.
lesson: Automation kills the narrowest task-specific jobs fast and the broader role slowly; know which one your customer holds.

quotes.text: Skills Lost To Modern Technology Are Many
quotes.speaker: Ray Higgins

quotes.text: Already the trade of the bookkeeper is threatened by the computer.
quotes.speaker: Ray Higgins

claim: Tiny portable mirrors feed women's vanity.
what_happened: Compact mirrors became an ordinary accessory, later folded into every phone's front camera.
lesson: Moral fears about personal grooming tools fade fast; the tool stays.

quotes.text: LITTLE AIDS FOR VAIN WOMEN.
ARE ROCK ISLAND WOMEN VAIN? ELEVATOR BOY DECIDES THEY ARE

claim: Women looking in hand mirrors while crossing the street are walking into streetcar accidents.
what_happened: Distracted pedestrians are a real hazard; the same complaint returned a century later about people looking at phones.
lesson: Distraction from a personal screen or mirror is a real cost; design for the moment of use, not just for the use.

quotes.text: Women Constantly Walk Into Danger.
quotes.speaker: R. S. Rowley, Chicago City Railway

quotes.text: they are apt to take oat their little mirror while standing in the middle of the car, track and rub it off.
quotes.speaker: R. S. Rowley, Chicago City Railway

claim: Cycling is producing a new insanity in women, making them extremely cruel.
what_happened: No 'bicycle insanity' was ever found; the bicycle became a symbol of women's independence.
lesson: When new freedom reaches a group that lacked it, expect a medical-sounding fear about that group.

quotes.text: Th doctors of . Franc are puzzled by a new mania which I aMIrtlng women who ride bicycle.
The feminine cyclists arc becoming extremely cruel.

claim: Scantily-clad bathers are indecent and must be ordered off the beach.
what_happened: Beach censorship collapsed by the 1930s; swimsuits kept shrinking and became mainstream fashion.
lesson: Decency rules policed by local officials rarely outlast a fashion customers want.

quotes.text: SCANTILY-CLAD BATHERS ORDERED OFF STRAND.

claim: Falling birth rates mean there will be no babies in the United States after 2020.
what_happened: About 3.6 million babies were born in the US in 2020; the extrapolation was absurd, though fertility did fall below replacement.
lesson: A straight-line extrapolation of a trend to zero is always wrong on the date, even when the trend's direction is right.

quotes.text: WILL BE NO BABIES AFTER YEAR 2020, SAYS WILLCOX
quotes.speaker: Prof. Walter F. Willcox, Cornell

claim: Children given too many toys lose resourcefulness and self-reliance.
what_happened: Toy abundance grew without the predicted collapse in character, though later studies found fewer toys can lengthen focused play.
lesson: Abundance fears hold a grain of truth about attention; products that do less, better, have a market inside the abundance.

quotes.text: TOO MANY TOYS Mrs. Cochran . Sounds Warning? to Mothers
quotes.speaker: Mrs. Joseph W. Cochran

quotes.text: It is the crime of thai age; it is a sin against lour ohildre.n

claim: Teddy bears replacing dolls will destroy girls' maternal instinct and drive race suicide.
what_happened: Chicago and Boston laughed it off at the time; the teddy bear became a permanent childhood staple alongside dolls.
lesson: When a fear is ridiculed the week it is aired, the product has already won the culture.

quotes.text: TEDDY BEAR DOOMS RACE Is Destroying Motherly Instincts in Little Girls, Says St. Joseph Priest.
quotes.speaker: Rev. Michael G. Esper

quotes.text: CHICAGO LAUGHS OVER TEDDY BEAR BAITING
TEDDY BEAR MENACES NATION.
quotes.speaker: Rev. Michael G. Esper

claim: The teddy bear will make the old-fashioned doll extinct, so schools should ban it.
what_happened: Dolls never went extinct; both toys sold for the next century.
lesson: A new product rarely kills the category it's compared to; it usually grows the shelf.

quotes.text: A BAS THE TEDDY BEAR. Ban Placed on Him to Save the Rationed Doll.
Fear has arisen in the minds of pedagogues and others that the old-fashioned doll will become extinct.
TEDDY BEAR A FAD. Hasn't Supplanted Doll in Childish Favor.

claim: Modern children are spoiled, bored, disrespectful and procrastinate because life is too easy.
what_happened: The same complaint recurs every generation; even the 1908 paper noted Uncle John's uncle said it about him.
lesson: 'Kids today' is a constant, not a signal; don't let it stand in for evidence about a product aimed at the young.

quotes.text: Are not children nowadays proverbially spoilt
YOUTHS OF TODAY PROCRASTINATE
quotes.speaker: Rev. J. W. Day

quotes.text: Have We Granted Children Too Much Freedom?

thing: jazz, movies, motor cars and sex novels
claim: Jazz, movies, the motor car and sex novels are producing a generation of wild youth.
what_happened: That 'wild' generation became the one that fought WWII; each blamed medium became mainstream.
lesson: A list of four new things blamed for one youth problem is a sign the blame is cultural, not causal.

quotes.text: 1926: Jazz, Movies, Motor Car, and Sex Novels Blamed for 'Wild Youth'

claim: Radio programmes and movies are distracting children from homework and lowering their grades.
what_happened: Displacement of homework and sleep by entertainment is real and recurred with TV and phones, but radio did not wreck schooling.
lesson: The displacement fear is the durable one: a new medium does take time from something, so say what your product's time replaces.

quotes.text: Many Things to Distract Child r From His Study
Movies and Radio Blamed for Poor Grades in School

claim: Beeping virtual pets are disrupting classrooms and must be barred from school.
what_happened: Schools banned them, the fad faded within two years, and no lasting harm followed.
lesson: A classroom ban is a sign of youth adoption, not of harm; fads end on their own schedule.

quotes.text: Pests in the classroom
quotes.speaker: Susan Semenak

claim: Pagers in schools are tools for drug deals and should be banned.
what_happened: Pagers really were used by dealers and many states banned them in schools; the device was soon replaced by the mobile phone, which raised the same debate.
lesson: A tool's early adopters include criminals; that is a misuse to design against, not a verdict on the tool.

quotes.text: School ban on beepers aims at curtailing drug deals

claim: Sensational cheap fiction turns boys' heads and drives them to run away and crime.
what_happened: Cheap fiction became pulp, comics and paperbacks; no rise in delinquency was ever traced to it.
lesson: Cheap, popular entertainment for the young is blamed for crime in every generation; the blame moves on to the next medium.

quotes.text: AGAIN THE YELLOW-BACK Two Gloucester Boy s' Heads Si . Turned by Flash Novels.
Everybody seems to be agreed in denouncing the penny dreadful.

claim: US crime magazines are causing Britain's wave of violence.
what_happened: The comics-and-crime-mag panic led to bans and codes; later research found no causal link to violence.
lesson: A foreign medium is an easy scapegoat for a domestic problem; check whether the timing actually lines up.

quotes.text: U.S. Crime Magazines Blamed For Britain's Wave of Violence

thing: reading in bed by electric light
claim: Reading in bed ruins the eyes and breeds slothfulness.
what_happened: Bedtime reading became a recommended habit; no eye harm was established.
lesson: Habits people look forward to all day are hard to talk them out of; build for the habit.

quotes.text: She had talked at length on the evil effects on eyes, its danger of slothful ness

claim: Motion pictures are a primary cause of America's rising divorce rate.
what_happened: Divorce rose for legal and economic reasons; films were never shown to drive it.
lesson: When a social trend has many causes, the newest medium gets blamed first; it is rarely the cause.

quotes.text: Booze, Lax Laws and Moving ; Pictures Blamed For Un-. . happy Marriages.
quotes.speaker: Southern Baptist Convention

claim: Movies, radio and cheap vaudeville are responsible for most present-day ills.
what_happened: The Vatican itself later ran Vatican Radio and blessed films; both media became mainstream.
lesson: Institutions that condemn a medium often end up broadcasting on it; plan for the critic to become a customer.

quotes.text: Movies, Radio Blamed For Many Modern Ills

claim: Mass media are standardising and flattening the public mind.
what_happened: Broadcast media did produce a more uniform national culture for decades, until cable and the internet fragmented it.
lesson: Homogenisation fears about a dominant channel tend to be right until the next channel fragments it.

quotes.text: Does This Modern Civilization Standardize Our Minds? Odegard Tells How Newspapers, Motion Pictures Schools and Radio Flatten the Public Mind

claim: Mass communication caters to the lazy half-wit.
what_happened: Mass media did chase the lowest common denominator, but literacy and education kept rising alongside it.
lesson: Every mass channel is accused of dumbing down; whether it does depends on what it displaces.

quotes.text: 1953: THE LAZY HALF-WIT AT LAST COMES INTO HIS OWN'

claim: Moving-picture machines are a new evil spreading immoral and obscene views.
what_happened: Film became the dominant art and entertainment form of the next century, managed by codes and ratings rather than suppression.
lesson: A new image medium's first moral panic is about its worst use; it settles into codes, not bans.

quotes.text: NEW EVIL TO CON BAT, Moving Picture Machines Furnished With Grossly Immoral Subjects.

claim: Talkies are only a craze; audiences will gladly return to the silent screen.
what_happened: Silent features were essentially gone by 1930.
lesson: When a medium adds a sense (sound, colour, interaction), 'fad' predictions die within a couple of years.

quotes.text: There Is no doubt that the "talkies" have come to stay. The pessimists and the conservatives, of course, have declared that they are only a "craze,"
quotes.speaker: Kenneth Wilkinson

claim: The talkies have thrown theatre musicians out of work.
what_happened: Recorded sound eliminated most of the roughly 20,000 US cinema musician jobs within a few years; the musicians' union fought it and lost.
lesson: Job-loss warnings about a specific trade are often exactly right even when aggregate employment is fine; serve the displaced trade.

quotes.text: tlie talkies, which have replaced so many musi- Clans.

claim: Riding elevators causes 'elevator sickness', brain fever and nervous disorders.
what_happened: Elevators became universal in tall buildings; brain fever from elevators never existed.
lesson: Motion discomfort on a new ride is real for minutes, not a disease; it fades with habituation and better engineering.

quotes.text: Cases of elevator sickness are on the increase,
quotes.speaker: Dr. E. C. Knowlton

claim: Removing elevator operators is partly to blame for New York's crime rise.
what_happened: Automatic elevators replaced nearly all operators by the 1960s; security moved to lobbies and cameras.
lesson: Removing a human from a role removes its informal duties too; replace those duties and the objection goes away.

quotes.text: Automatic Elevator Blamed in Part For Crime Rise
quotes.speaker: Alice Hughes

claim: 'Canned' love-song music on the phonograph wrecks homes and marriages.
what_happened: The phonograph became a household fixture; no wave of record-driven elopements followed.
lesson: One lurid anecdote is not a trend; check whether the headline has a second case.

quotes.text: "CANNED" MUSIC WRECKS HOME PHONOGRAPH IS THE INNOCENT CAUSE- OF DESTRUCTION OF HAPPINESS.

claim: A neighbour's loud gramophone is an intolerable nuisance that courts should restrain.
what_happened: The court brokered a compromise on volume; noise from personal audio remained a real but manageable neighbour dispute.
lesson: Externalities of a personal device end up governed by norms and volume knobs; ship the knob.

quotes.text: GRAMOPHONE IS WITNESS IN COURT COMPLAINED OF AS NUISANCE TO NEIGHBORHOOD

claim: A machine that writes from the voice will do away with stenographers.
what_happened: Stenographers thrived for most of the century; speech recognition only began displacing transcription work in the 2010s.
lesson: Inventors announce job replacement decades early; the direction can be right while the timing is wrong by a lifetime.

quotes.text: Stenographers Doomed by Machine.
A machine which the inventor claims will do away with stenographers has been invented by Joseph McCaulI of this city.

claim: The typewriter will have its brief day as a fad and then be thrown aside.
what_happened: The typewriter became the core office machine for a century and opened clerical work to women.
lesson: Even inventors misjudge their own product's staying power; adoption, not the founder's mood, is the signal.

quotes.text: I fear the typewriter will have its brief day as a fad and then be thrown aside,
quotes.speaker: Christopher Sholes

claim: Phones that transmit the caller's face are a dreadful prospect.
what_happened: Video calling arrived in the 2000s–2020s and is universal, but camera fatigue and camera-off norms show the discomfort was real.
lesson: Being seen is a cost users weigh; make the camera optional and the feature wins anyway.

quotes.text: Will Science Develop Phone Photography?
quotes.speaker: N. P. Babcock

quotes.text: leads naturally to the dreadful thought that mankind mlgnt regard with favor a promise of telephone photography
quotes.speaker: N. P. Babcock

claim: Video phones won't catch on because people must tidy their hair before answering.
what_happened: Dedicated video phones did flop through the 1990s; video calling won only once it was free, optional and built into phones and laptops.
lesson: Friction kills a standalone device that the same feature later wins on as a free add-on; bundle the awkward feature.

quotes.text: An experiment with AT&T PicturePhones found them ringing an average of 11 times while users tidied their hair and desks.
quotes.speaker: Elizabeth Hanscom

claim: The telephone breeds a new nuisance, the 'telephone fool', and a malady called telephonitis.
what_happened: Phone etiquette settled into norms and the telephone became universal.
lesson: Bad manners on a new channel are a phase; norms form once everyone is on it.

quotes.text: TELEPHONE FOOL," ROSE MARION FINDS, ONE OF GREATEST NUISANCES
quotes.speaker: Rose Marion

quotes.text: Mr. Jarr Describes a New Malady Known to Science as 'Telephonitis.'

claim: The telephone is a menace to the Sultan's life and must be banned, even reading about it.
what_happened: Turkey let foreign firms build service in 1911; the ban had only delayed the country's phone network.
lesson: Rulers who ban a communication tool to protect their control only delay it, and lose the head start.

quotes.text: Telephones were banned as a menace to the life of the Sultan, and even to read literature pertaining to the telephone was forbidden.

claim: College girls are addicted to sending telegrams.
what_happened: The telegram faded to the phone; heavy messaging by young people became ordinary with each later channel.
lesson: Young people messaging a lot is the oldest 'addiction' headline; it signals the channel's market, not a pathology.

quotes.text: Wellesley Co-eds Are Addicted to Telegrams

claim: A 'photographic mania' can seize anyone overnight.
what_happened: Snapshot photography became a universal hobby, then a phone feature.
lesson: When the press calls a hobby a mania, it's describing product-market fit.

quotes.text: It is impossible to tell over night wlto may be attacked by tie photogTaphio mania.

claim: Machines are taking jobs faster than new industries can absorb the workers.
what_happened: Specific trades were wiped out, but total employment recovered after the Depression and grew with new industries.
lesson: Automation fears are right about the trade and usually wrong about the economy; build for the displaced worker's next job.

claim: The dial telephone has thrown thousands of girls (operators) out of work.
what_happened: Mechanical switching steadily eliminated operator jobs; research found displaced cohorts moved into other work rather than lasting unemployment.
lesson: The trade-level job loss was real and complete; the consolation is that new entrants simply chose other jobs.

claim: Developing hydro power in a coal country is suicidal folly and a job-destroying Frankenstein.
what_happened: TVA, Boulder (Hoover) and Grand Coulee dams electrified whole regions and helped power WWII industry.
lesson: When the warning about a new energy source comes from the old one's utility, weigh it as a business interest.

quotes.text: Hydro-electric power is a “modern Frankenstein”
quotes.speaker: A. M. Beebee, Rochester Gas and Electric

claim: The electronic brain can't think and shouldn't be humanised; it's only a calculator.
what_happened: Correct about 1955 hardware; seventy years on, whether machines 'think' is the central debate around AI.
lesson: 'It's just a calculator' can be right about today's machine and wrong about its descendants; build for the descendant.

quotes.text: It's Fine Computer, but It Can't Think and Lee Wilcox Won't 'Humanize' It
quotes.speaker: Lee Wilcox, Monsanto

claim: The home computer may be going the way of video games, a dying fad.
what_happened: Home PCs reached most US households by 2000, and video games became bigger than film.
lesson: A slump after the first hype wave is not death; even a co-founder can mistake the trough for the end.

quotes.text: Apple wizard says computer 'fad' dying
The home computer may be going the way of video games, which are a dying fad.
quotes.speaker: Steve Wozniak

claim: Sky-high hype for the iPhone could come back to bite Apple.
what_happened: The iPhone became the most profitable product in history and made Apple the world's most valuable company.
lesson: 'Expectations are too high' is a hedge, not an analysis; ask whether the product creates a new category.

quotes.text: High expectations of iPhone could bite Apple
quotes.speaker: Jordan Robertson

claim: Portable headphone stereos are ushering in an age of isolation.
what_happened: Personal audio became universal; public life did grow more privatised, a complaint now made about AirPods and phones.
lesson: Users buy isolation on purpose; the product that lets them choose when to tune out wins.

quotes.text: Sales of portable stereos boom, ushering in an age of isolation

thing: cell phones, call waiting, voice mail and the Walkman
claim: Personal technology is making people uncivil.
what_happened: Every named device became universal; phone etiquette norms partly formed (silence in theatres) and partly didn't.
lesson: New devices break old manners before new ones form; products that build in the courtesy (silent mode) age best.

quotes.text: Technology is making us uncivil
quotes.speaker: Lewis Beale

claim: Too much artificial light and white surfaces are damaging eyes; over half of schoolchildren have vision defects.
what_happened: The white-ceiling theory was wrong, but modern research ties the myopia epidemic to indoor life and too little daylight.
lesson: A wrong mechanism can sit on top of a real effect; test the effect separately from the story told about it.

quotes.text: Too Much Artificial Light, White Ceilings and White Clothes.
quotes.speaker: Dr. R. Kendrick Smith

quotes.text: Babies should not be dressed J in white.

claim: Modern art depicting slums and degradation is degenerate.
what_happened: Modernist and realist art moved into the major museums and the canon.
lesson: Taste-makers' contempt for new art forms is a weak predictor; audiences and later critics decide.

quotes.text: MODERN ART DEGENERATING SAYS EXPERT

claim: Horseless carriages are just the latest fad people will outgrow.
what_happened: The Model T arrived in 1908 and the horse was gone from city streets by the 1920s.
lesson: Toys for the rich become infrastructure once the price falls; judge by the cost curve, not by early buyers.

claim: Automobiles are a danger and must be banned from public parks.
what_happened: The bans fell as cars spread, but cars went on to kill tens of thousands a year, and many cities later re-closed park roads to traffic.
lesson: Early local bans fail against a useful machine, but the safety concern behind them often comes back as regulation.

claim: Chain stores will destroy independent grocers and drain wealth from local communities.
what_happened: Chains did displace most independent grocers and won on price; the campaign produced anti-chain taxes and the Robinson-Patman Act but never stopped the shift.
lesson: Incumbents can be right that a model will hurt them and still lose; customers choose price and convenience over solidarity.
